Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Klemmbrett

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): klemmen

ordentlich.notes: Means both 'tidy, neat' (ein ordentliches Zimmer) and colloquially 'proper, hefty, a good solid amount' (eine ordentliche Portion, Es regnet ordentlich!).

ordnung.etymology: From Middle High German ordenunge and Old High German ordinunga ('arrangement, sequence, rule, rank'), action/state noun in -ung from ordnen (OHG ordinōn 'to arrange, put in order', borrowed from Latin ōrdināre, from ōrdō 'row, rank, order').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Ordnung
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Ordnung

ort.etymology: From Middle High German and Old High German ort ('sharp point of a weapon, corner, edge, extremity, place'), from Proto-Germanic *uzdaz ('point, tip', cognate with Old English ord 'spear-point, beginning'); shifted in Late MHG from 'corner/point' to 'spot, place, town'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Ort
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Ort

paar.etymology: From Middle High German and Old High German pār ('two things of equal kind, pair'), borrowed from Latin pār (neuter plural paria 'equals, a matching pair'); lowercase ein paar ('a few') developed in Early New High German.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Paar
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Paar

packung.etymology: Action and concrete noun in -ung derived from packen ('to pack, wrap into a bundle', borrowed in Late MHG from Middle Dutch/Middle Low German pakken), denoting a package or pack.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Packung
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Packung

paket.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century as a postal and trade term from French paquet ('small bundle, parcel'), diminutive of Old French pac (which was itself borrowed from Middle Dutch pak 'bundle').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Paket
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Paket

panik.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th/19th century via French panique from Ancient Greek panikón (deîma) ('sudden groundless terror sent by the woodland god Pan', from Pán).

history.meaning: of the god Pan; sudden terror

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Panik
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Panik

papier.etymology: From Late Middle High German papīr ('paper'), borrowed via Old French papier or Medieval Latin papīrum from Classical Latin papȳrus and Ancient Greek pápyros ('Nile papyrus sedge and writing material').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Papier
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Papier

papierbuch.etymology: Determinative compound of Papier ('paper', Late MHG papīr) and Buch ('book', MHG buoch, OHG buoh), originally distinguishing paper codices from parchment manuscripts, now a paper book or ledger.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Papier
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Papier

papieretikett.etymology: Determinative compound of Papier ('paper', Late MHG papīr) and Etikett ('attached label, tag', borrowed in the 18th c. from French étiquette 'small slip of paper or parchment attached to a document bag').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Etikett
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Etikett

papierkram.etymology: Colloquial compound of Papier ('paper, documents', Late MHG papīr) and Kram ('small wares, odds and ends, clutter', MHG krām 'merchant's tent/booth, small goods'), denoting tedious paperwork or red tape.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Papierkram
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Papierkram

papierlaterne.etymology: Determinative compound of Papier ('paper', Late MHG papīr) and Laterne ('lantern', MHG laterne < Latin lanterna).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Laterne
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Laterne

papierschild.etymology: Determinative compound of Papier ('paper', Late MHG papīr) and Schild ('sign, label, placard', MHG schilt, OHG scilt).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Schild
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Schild

paragraf.etymology: From Late Middle High German paragraf ('section mark §, numbered article of a legal code'), borrowed via Medieval Latin paragraphus from Ancient Greek parágraphos ('marginal stroke marking a section break', from paraghráphein 'to write beside').

history.meaning: marginal stroke marking a break in text

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Paragraf
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Paragraf

passen.etymology: From Late Middle High German passen ('to be suitable, fit, wait for'), borrowed via Middle Dutch passen from Old French passer ('to pass, go through, suit', from Vulgar Latin *passāre, from Latin passus 'step').

history.meaning: to fit, suit, watch out for

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): passen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): passen

passend.etymology: Lexicalized present participle of passen ('to fit, suit', Late MHG passen), used adjectivally for 'fitting, suitable, matching, appropriate'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): passend
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): passend

peng.etymology: Recorded in DWDS/Pfeifer (19th c.) as an expressive sound-imitative interjection echoing a sharp bang or shot.

history.meaning: 19th-c. expressive sound-imitation of a sharp report, pop, or gunshot

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): peng
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): peng

peng.notes: German's classic comic-strip and spoken sound effect for a sudden pop, burst balloon, or blown fuse ('Bang! / Pop!').

pension.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French pension ('board and lodging payment, boarding house'), from Latin pēnsiō ('payment, weighing out'). In German it names a cosy, small guesthouse.

sources.title: DWDS: Pension
Wiktionary: Pension (German)

per.etymology: Preposition ('by, via, by means of, as of') borrowed in the 15th/16th century through Italian and Latin commercial correspondence from Latin per ('through, by means of').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): per
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): per

perfekt.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th/16th century (first in Latin grammar for the perfect tense, then generally for 'flawless, accomplished') from Latin perfectus ('completed, fully accomplished', past participle of perficere).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): perfekt
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): perfekt

pfeil.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace Pfeil through OHG pfīl and MHG pfīl as an early West Germanic borrowing from Latin pīlum ('heavy javelin'), showing the High German shift of p- to pf-.

cognates.meaning: heavy pointed timber driven into ground (< Old English pīl, from the same Latin pīlum!)

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Pfeil
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Pfeil

pfeil.notes: Compare Dutch pijl and German Pfeil: because Roman pīlum entered Germanic BEFORE the High German consonant shift, p- turned into pf- and long ī into ei!

pflanze.etymology: From Middle High German pflanze and Old High German pflanza ('shoot, slip, seedling, plant'), borrowed before the High German consonant shift (showing p- > pf- and -t- > -z-) from Latin planta ('sprout, cutting, seedling').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Pflanze
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Pflanze

pinsel.etymology: From Middle High German bensel, pinsel ('painter's brush'), borrowed via Old French pincel from Vulgar Latin *pēnicellus, diminutive of Latin pēniculus ('brush, little tail').

history.meaning: little tail -> tuft of hair used as a painter's brush

cognates.meaning: originally 'fine camel-hair paintbrush' before shifting to graphite sticks!

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Pinsel
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Pinsel

pinsel.notes: Big false-friend alert! Der Pinsel is a 'paintbrush / pastry brush' (keeping the original medieval sense of Old French pincel), whereas an English 'pencil' is der Bleistift!

pinzette.etymology: 18th-century borrowing from French pincette ('small tongs, tweezers'), diminutive of pince from pincer ('to pinch').

cognates.meaning: gripping tool (and pinch, from the same French root)

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Pinzette
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Pinzette

pinzette.notes: Singular feminine in German (eine Pinzette, die Pinzette), unlike English plural-only 'tweezers'!

plan.etymology: In the sense 'design, blueprint, schedule, intention', borrowed in the 18th century from French plan ('ground plan, flat projection, scheme', from Latin plānus 'flat, level'); reinforced by older MHG plān ('open field, plain').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Plan
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Plan

planen.etymology: Denominal weak verb formed in the 18th/19th century from Plan ('design, project, schedule', from French plan), meaning 'to plan, design, schedule'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): planen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): planen

platz.etymology: From Middle High German platz, plaz ('open square in a town, dancing place, spot'), borrowed via Old French place / Medieval Latin placea from Latin platēa ('broad street, courtyard', from Greek plateîa [hodós] 'broad way').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Platz
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Platz

plus.etymology: Borrowed in the late 15th century by Renaissance mathematicians from Latin plūs ('more', comparative of multus 'much'), originally a shorthand for 'and more' in addition.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): plus
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): plus

polieren.etymology: From Middle High German polieren, palieren ('to smooth, burnish, polish'), borrowed via Old French polir directly from Latin polīre ('to smooth, polish, refine').

cognates.meaning: via Old French stem poliss- of the same verb polir

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): polieren
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): polieren

polieren.notes: Forms its past participle without ge-: Ich habe das Messing poliert ('I polished the brass').

porzellansicherung.etymology: Determinative compound of Porzellan ('porcelain', borrowed in the 16th c. from Italian porcellana 'cowrie shell; translucent ceramic') and Sicherung ('electrical fuse; safety device', from sichern 'to secure').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Porzellan
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Porzellan

postkarte.etymology: Compound coined in 1870 (by Heinrich von Stephan for the North German Confederation postal service, replacing Correspondenzkarte) from Post ('postal service', from Italian posta) and Karte ('card').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Postkarte
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Postkarte

preis.etymology: From Middle High German prīs ('praise, glory, prize; value, price'), borrowed in the 12th century from Old French pris ('value, price, honor, reward', from Late Latin pretiō / Classical Latin pretium 'worth, price').

history.meaning: worth, price, praise, prize (< Latin pretium)

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Preis
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Preis

prise.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French prise ('pinch taken between thumb and forefinger, grasp'), substantivised feminine past participle of prendre ('to take', Latin prehendere).

history.meaning: a taking; pinch held between thumb and finger
tiny pinch of salt, spice, or snuff; fresh sea breeze

cognates.meaning: captured ship/booty (from the same French prise 'a taking')

rootFamily.gloss: tip of a knife (related tiny recipe measure)

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Prise
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Prise

prise.notes: Every German baking recipe calls for eine Prise Salz ('a pinch of salt' — literally 'one thumb-and-finger take'!).

privat.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Latin prīvātus ('set apart from the state, belonging to an individual, personal', originally past participle of prīvāre 'to strip, set apart', from prīvus 'single, one's own').

history.meaning: not in public office, personal, private

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): privat
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): privat

pro.etymology: Distributive preposition ('per, for each') borrowed in the 15th/16th century through Latin chancery and mercantile usage from Latin prō ('for, in proportion to, on behalf of').

history.meaning: for, on behalf of, in proportion to

probewoche.etymology: Determinative compound of Probe ('trial, test, rehearsal', Late MHG prōbe, borrowed from Medieval Latin proba 'proof, test') and Woche ('week', MHG woche, OHG wehha).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Probe
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Probe

probieren.etymology: From Middle High German probieren, prōbieren ('to test, examine, prove'), borrowed from Latin probāre ('to test, find good, approve', from probus 'good, upright') or Old French prover.

problem.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century via Latin problēma from Ancient Greek próblēma ('something thrown forward, obstacle, question proposed for solution', from probállein 'to throw before').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Problem

prozent.etymology: From Italian per cento / Neo-Latin pro cento ('per hundred') in commercial arithmetic.

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Prozent

prüfen.etymology: From Middle High German prüeven, brüeven ('to test, examine, reckon, perceive, prove'), borrowed in the 12th century from Old French prover ('to test, prove', from Latin probāre), an earlier doublet of probieren.

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Prüfer

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Puderzucker
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Puderzucker

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Punkt
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Punkt

putzen.etymology: From Late Middle High German butzen, putzen ('to trim a candle wick, wipe clean, adorn'), originally 'to remove the lump/mucus/burnt wick' from Butzen ('lump, core, snivel, wick-end', MHG butze).

history.meaning: to snuff a wick, clean, polish

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Pünktlichkeit

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Quittung

rabatt.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century as a mercantile term from Italian rabatto ('deduction from a price, discount'), verbal noun from rabattere ('to beat back, deduct, knock off', from ri- + abbattere).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Rabatt
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Rabatt

rad.etymology: From Middle High German rat (gen. rades) and Old High German rad ('wheel'), from Proto-Germanic *raþą, from PIE *róth₂os ('wheel, chariot', from *reth₂- 'to run, roll'), cognate with Latin rota, Old Irish roth, and Sanskrit rátha-.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Rad
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Rad

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Gitter

raten.etymology: From Middle High German rāten and Old High German rātan ('to advise, counsel, deliberate, conjecture, guess'), reduplicating strong verb from Proto-Germanic *rēdaną (PIE *h₁reh₁dʰ- 'to arrange, succeed'), cognate with Old English rǣdan (English 'read').

raum.etymology: From Middle High German and Old High German rūm ('open space, clearance, room to move'), from Proto-Germanic *rūmaz (substantivized from the adjective *rūmaz 'spacious, wide'), cognate with English 'room'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Raum

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): rechts

rede.etymology: From Middle High German rede and Old High German reda, redia ('account, reason, speech, discourse, conversation'), from Proto-Germanic *raþjō ('reckoning, account', cognate with Gothic raþjō 'number, account' and Latin ratiō).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Regal
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Regal

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Regel
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Regel

satz.etymology: From Middle High German saz, satz ('place where something is set, position, stake, ordinance, jump, sentence'), deverbal noun from setzen ('to set, place, compose', OHG sezzen).

schuld.etymology: From Middle High German schulde, schult and Old High German sculda ('obligation, debt, tribute, offense, guilt'), dental abstract noun (*skuldi-) from the preterite-present verb sollen ('shall, to owe', OHG scolan, Proto-Germanic *skulaną).

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Schuld

schulden.etymology: From Middle High German schulden and Old High German sculdōn ('to owe, be obligated, deserve'), denominal weak verb derived from Schuld ('debt, obligation', OHG sculda).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): schulden
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): schulden

schule.etymology: From Middle High German schuole and Old High German scuola ('school, instruction'), borrowed in the monastic period from Medieval Latin scōla (Classical Latin schola 'leisure given to learning, lecture, school'), from Ancient Greek scholḗ ('leisure, philosophical discussion, school').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Schule
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Schule

schulter.etymology: From Middle High German schulter and Old High German scultirra, scultra ('shoulder'), a West Germanic anatomical term (*skuldrō, cognate with Old English sculdor, English 'shoulder') of uncertain pre-Germanic etymology.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Schulter
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Schulter

schwamm.etymology: Old High German swam, Middle High German swam ('fungus, porous sponge'), from Proto-Germanic *swammaz, cognate with English swamp.

cognates.meaning: spongy wet ground (from the exact same root *swamm- / *swamp-!)

rootFamily.gloss: 'let's wipe the slate clean / forget about it!'

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Schwamm
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Schwamm

schwamm.notes: Plural with umlaut: der Schwamm -> die Schwämme; in Bavarian/Austrian German, Schwammerl still means 'mushrooms', preserving the ancient dual meaning!

schwarz.etymology: From Middle High German and Old High German swarz ('black, dark'), from Proto-Germanic *swartaz ('black, dark-colored', cognate with Old English sweart, English 'swarthy'), from PIE *swordo- ('dirty, dark').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): schwarz
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): schwarz

schwarzweißfoto.etymology: Compound of copulative adjective schwarzweiß ('black-and-white') and Foto (clipping of Fotografie, Greek phōs 'light' + gráphein 'to draw'); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Schwarzweißfoto.

cognates.meaning: dark-complexioned (from Old English sweart, cognate with schwarz!)

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Schwarzweißfoto
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Schwarzweißfoto

schwarzweißfoto.notes: May also be written hyphenated as Schwarz-Weiß-Foto under reformed orthography; plural die Schwarzweißfotos.

schwelle.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace Schwelle through OHG swelli and MHG swelle ('foundation beam, sill'), exact cognate with English sill.

cognates.meaning: windowsill or doorsill (< Old English syll, exact cognate!)

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Schwelle
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Schwelle

schwelle.notes: Not related to schwellen ('to swell')! Die Schwelle is the timber beam under a doorway (cognate with English sill) — über die Schwelle treten ('to step across the threshold').

schwer.etymology: From Middle High German swære, swār and Old High German swāri, swār ('heavy, burdensome, grievous, difficult'), from Proto-Germanic *swērijaz ('heavy, weighty'), related to Latin sērius ('grave, earnest').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): schwer
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): schwer

schön.etymology: From Middle High German schœne and Old High German scōni ('shining, bright, fair, beautiful'), originally a verbal adjective meaning 'worth looking at, notable' from Proto-Germanic *skaunijaz, derived from the root of schauen ('to look, behold'). Cognate with English 'sheen'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): schön
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): schön

schüchtern.etymology: Early New High German schüchtern ('shy, timid, easily frightened'), derived with an adjectival -ern suffix from Middle High German schiuhen ('to frighten, shun, shy away from') and Old High German sciuhen, related to scheu ('shy').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): schüchtern
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): schüchtern

schützen.etymology: From Middle High German schützen ('to dam up water, enclose, protect, defend'), originally a technical term for holding back water with a floodgate (Schütze) and thereby shielding land, related to schießen ('to shoot, push a bolt').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): schützen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): schützen

sechs.etymology: From Middle High German and Old High German sehs ('six'), from Proto-Germanic *sehs (cognate with English 'six'), from Proto-Indo-European *sweks ('six', cf. Latin sex, Greek héx).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): sechs
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): sechs

sechzehn.etymology: From Middle High German sehzehen and Old High German sehszehen ('sixteen'), a compound numeral combining sechs ('six', with loss of -s- before z-) and zehn ('ten').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): sechzehn
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): sechzehn

sehen.etymology: From Middle High German sehen and Old High German sehan ('to see, look, perceive'), from Proto-Germanic *sehwaną (cognate with English 'see'), from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- ('to follow with the eyes, notice, see').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): sehen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): sehen

sehr.etymology: From Middle High German sēre, sēr ('painfully, sorely, violently, very') and Old High German sēro ('painfully, sorely'), adverbial form of the adjective sēr ('wounded, painful'), from Proto-Germanic *sairaz (cognate with English 'sore'); semantically bleached to an intensifier ('very').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): sehr
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): sehr

seife.etymology: From Middle High German seife and Old High German seifa, seipfa ('soap, resin'), from Proto-Germanic *saipwōn- ('dripping resin, reddish hair-dye or soap', cognate with Old English sāpe, English 'soap').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Seife
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Seife

seifenwasser.etymology: Determinative compound of Seife ('soap', OHG seifa, with linking -n-) and Wasser ('water', OHG wazzar, MHG wazzer), denoting soapy water or suds.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Seifenwasser
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Seifenwasser

sein.etymology: Modern sein merges three ancient Indo-European roots: *bheu- ('grow, become') in bin and bist, *es- ('be') in ist and sind, and *wes- ('dwell, remain', OHG wesan) in war and gewesen. A separate homonymous stem OHG sīn produced the possessive sein ('his/its').

history.meaning: to be; to dwell or remain

sources.title: DWDS: sein
Wiktionary: sein (German)

seit.etymology: From Middle High German and Old High German sīt ('since, after, later'), originally a comparative adverb meaning 'later' from Proto-Germanic *sīþiz ('more lately', cognate with Old English sīþ, Gothic seiþus 'late').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): seit
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): seit

seitdem.etymology: Univerbation of the preposition seit ('since', MHG sīt) and the dative demonstrative pronoun dem ('that', MHG dem), originally a phrase sīt dem ('since that [time]').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): seitdem
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): seitdem

seite.etymology: From Middle High German sīte and Old High German sīta ('flank, side'), from Proto-Germanic *sīdōn- ('long part, flank, side', cognate with English 'side'), derived from the adjective *sīdaz ('long, hanging down').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Seite
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Seite

seitengriff.etymology: Determinative compound of Seite ('side', OHG sīta, with linking -n-) and Griff ('handle, grip', OHG grif, MHG grif, verbal noun to greifen 'to grasp').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Seitengriff
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Seitengriff

sekunde.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th/16th century from Medieval Latin secunda, shortened from pars minuta secunda ('second diminished part', the second sexagesimal subdivision of an hour or degree after the minute), from Latin secundus ('following, second').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Sekunde
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Sekunde

selb.etymology: From Middle High German selp, selber and Old High German selb ('same, self'), from Proto-Germanic *selbaz ('self, same', cognate with English 'self', Gothic silba).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): selb
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): selb

selbst.etymology: From Middle High German selbest, selbs, originating as the genitive singular selbes of selp ('self', OHG selb) with an excrescent final -t added in Late Middle High German (parallel to obst, papst, sonst).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): selbst
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): selbst

selbstverständlich.etymology: 19th-century compound adjective built from the phrase (von) selbst verstehen ('to be understood of itself'), combining selbst ('itself', MHG selbest) and verständlich ('understandable', from Verstand 'understanding', MHG verstant).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): selbstverständlich
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): selbstverständlich

seltsam.etymology: Reshaped by folk-etymological assimilation to the suffix -sam from Middle High German seltsæne and Old High German seltsāni ('rarely seen, strange, wondrous'), a compound of selt- (from selten 'rare') and *-sāni ('seen', related to sehen 'to see', cognate with Old English seldsīene).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): seltsam
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): seltsam

service.etymology: Borrowed twice: in the sense 'tableware set' (17th c., neuter) from French service, and in the sense 'customer service, maintenance' (20th c., masculine) from English service (via Old French servise), both ultimately from Latin servitium ('slavery, service', from servus 'servant, slave').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Service
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Service

servieren.etymology: Borrowed via French servir ('to serve at table') from Latin servīre, integrated with the standard German loan-verb suffix -ieren.

sources.title: DWDS: servieren
Wiktionary: servieren (German)

servieren.notes: Verbs ending in -ieren form their past participle without ge- (serviert).

serviette.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from French serviette ('table napkin, towel'), a derivative of servir ('to serve at table'), from Latin servīre ('to serve').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Serviette
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Serviette

setzen.etymology: Old High German sezzen and Middle High German setzen originated as the causative of sitzen ('to sit'), literally meaning 'to cause to sit, place'. Used reflexively (sich setzen), it means 'to sit down'.

sich.etymology: Continues Old High German sih and Middle High German sich, the inherited third-person reflexive pronoun; also used in modern German with polite Sie.

sources.title: DWDS: sich
Wiktionary: sich (German)

sicher.etymology: From Middle High German sicher and Old High German sihhur ('free from care, safe, certain, reliable'), an early West Germanic borrowing from Latin sēcūrus ('carefree, untroubled, safe', from sē- 'without' + cūra 'care').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): sicher
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): sicher

sicherheit.etymology: From Middle High German sicherheit and Old High German sihhurheit ('freedom from danger, certainty, guarantee, security'), derived from sicher ('safe, certain') with the abstract noun suffix -heit.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Sicherheit
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Sicherheit

sie.etymology: Old High German siu / sī ('she') and sie ('they') converged in modern lowercase sie. In Early New High German, capitalized third-person plural Sie became the standard polite form of address for one or more adults.

DWDS: Sie

sie.notes: Capitalization in writing (Sie, Ihnen, Ihr) distinguishes polite 'you' from 'she' or 'they'.

sieben.etymology: From Middle High German siben and Old High German sibun ('seven'), from Proto-Germanic *sebun (cognate with English 'seven'), from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥ ('seven', cf. Latin septem, Greek heptá).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): sieben
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): sieben

silbern.etymology: From Middle High German silberīn and Old High German silbarīn ('made of silver, silvery'), material adjective formed with suffix -īn (> -ern) from Silber ('silver', OHG silbar, Proto-Germanic *silubrą).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): silbern
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): silbern

singend.etymology: Present participle of singen ('to sing'), from Middle High German singende and Old High German singanti, from the strong verb singan (Proto-Germanic *singwaną 'to sing, chant').

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): singend

cognates.meaning: long-grade cousin (via Old Norse sæti) from the same root *sed-

rootFamily.gloss: seat (in a café, train, or theater)

sitzen.etymology: From Middle High German sitzen and Old High German sizzen ('to sit, reside'), from Proto-Germanic *sitjaną (cognate with English 'sit'), a j-present from Proto-Indo-European *sed- ('to sit', cf. Latin sedēre).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): sitzen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): sitzen

so.etymology: Continues Old and Middle High German sō ('in this manner, thus'), used both for manner ('like this') and degree ('so quiet').

Wiktionary: so (German)

sobald.etymology: Univerbation of Middle High German sō balde ('as quickly as, as soon as'), combining sō ('so, as', OHG sō) and balde ('boldly, quickly, soon', OHG baldo).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): sobald
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): sobald

sofort.etymology: Early New High German univerbation (17th c.) of so fort ('right away, immediately'), combining so ('thus, right') and fort ('forth, onward', MHG vort).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): sofort
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): sofort

sogar.etymology: Early New High German univerbation (17th c.) of the intensifying phrase so gar ('so completely, even'), from so ('so', OHG sō) and gar ('ready, completely, wholly', OHG garo).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): sogar
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): sogar

solange.etymology: Univerbation of the correlative phrase so lange ('as long as'), from Middle High German sō lange and Old High German sō lango, combining sō ('as, so') and the temporal adverb lange ('long').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): solange
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): solange

solcher.etymology: From Middle High German solich, solch and Old High German solīh, sulīh ('such, of this kind'), from Proto-Germanic *swalīkaz ('so-formed, such', cognate with English 'such', Gothic swaleiks), a compound of *swa ('so') + *līką ('body, form').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): solcher
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): solcher

sollen.etymology: From Old High German scolan / solan and Middle High German soln ('to owe, be obliged to'), related to Schuld ('debt, fault') and English 'shall / should'.

sources.title: DWDS: sollen
Wiktionary: sollen (German)

sommer.etymology: From Middle High German sumer and Old High German sumar ('summer'), from Proto-Germanic *sumaraz (cognate with English 'summer'), from Proto-Indo-European *semh₂- ('summer, half-year').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Sommer
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Sommer

sommergast.etymology: Determinative compound of Sommer ('summer', OHG sumar, MHG sumer) and Gast ('guest, visitor', OHG gast, MHG gast), denoting a summer visitor or vacationer.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Sommergast
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Sommergast

sonne.etymology: Continues Old High German sunna and Middle High German sunne ('sun, sunlight'), from Proto-Germanic *sunnǭ (< PIE *sóh₂wl̥), lowering u to o before double nasal in Central and New High German.

history.meaning: sun, sunshine (with Central German u > o before nn)

cognates.meaning: from the l-stem of the same heteroclite PIE *sóh₂wl̥!

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Sonne

sonne.notes: Notice the regular u -> o shift before nn/mm in German vs. English: Sonne = sun, Sommer = summer, Nonne = nun, gewonnen = won, geschwommen = swum!

sonnenhof.etymology: Toponymic and architectural compound name from Sonne ('sun', OHG sunna, MHG sunne, with weak genitive/linking -n-) and Hof ('courtyard, estate, inn', OHG hof, MHG hof), literally 'sunny courtyard/inn'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Sonnenhof
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Sonnenhof

sonnenlicht.etymology: From Middle High German sunnenlieht ('sunlight'), a compound of Sonne ('sun', OHG sunna, MHG sunne) and Licht ('light', OHG lioht, MHG lieht).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Sonnenlicht
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Sonnenlicht

sonnig.etymology: Derived from Sonne ('sun', MHG sunne, OHG sunna) with the adjectival suffix -ig (Early New High German sonnig, replacing older MHG sunneclīch 'sunny').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): sonnig
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): sonnig

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Sonntag

sonntagsbrot.etymology: Determinative compound of Sonntag ('Sunday', OHG sunnūntag, with adverbial/genitival -s-) and Brot ('bread', OHG brōt, MHG brōt), referring to finer bread baked for Sunday.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Sonntagsbrot
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Sonntagsbrot

sonst.etymology: From Middle High German sunst, sus, sust ('thus, in such a way, otherwise, else') and Old High German sus ('thus, so'), with secondary nasal insertion (-n-) and excrescent final -t in Late Middle High German.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): sonst
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): sonst

sorge.etymology: From Middle High German sorge and Old High German sorga, sworga ('worry, grief, care, anxiety'), from Proto-Germanic *surgō ('care, sorrow', cognate with Old English sorh, English 'sorrow').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Sorge
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Sorge

spalte.etymology: Old High German spalta ('cleft, division'), from spalten ('to split, divide into columns').

history.meaning: fissure, slit; vertical column of a two-column manuscript page!

cognates.meaning: woodworking term 'brittle/split wood' (and dialectal spald 'to split')

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Spalte

spalten.etymology: Old High German spaltan, Middle High German spalten, from Proto-Germanic *spaldaną ('to cleave, split').

cognates.meaning: archaic/technical 'to split, cleave' (< Middle Dutch spalden)
borrowed from Middle Dutch splitten (distant cousin from the same *spel- 'cleave' family)

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): spalten

spalten.notes: Conjugates regularly weak in the past (spaltete), while keeping BOTH historical strong gespalten (especially figurative: eine gespaltene Meinung) and weak gespaltet (for physical wood: Holz gespaltet/gespalten).

spaziergang.etymology: Early New High German compound of spazieren ('to stroll, walk for pleasure', MHG spazieren, borrowed in the 14th c. from Italian spaziare < Latin spatiārī 'to walk about, promenade', from spatium 'space, walk') and Gang ('walk, gait', OHG and MHG gang).

history.meaning: to walk about, take a walk

teetasse.etymology: Compound of Tee ('tea', via Dutch thee from Hokkien tê) and Tasse ('cup', from French tasse), denoting a teacup.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Teetasse
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Teetasse

teilen.etymology: Old High German teilen, Middle High German teilen ('to divide into parts, share'), denominal verb from Teil ('part').

cognates.meaning: originally 'to divide, distribute shares' (as in 'deal cards'!)

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): teilen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): teilen

teilen.notes: Covers BOTH 'to split/divide' (durch zwei teilen) AND warm 'to share' (Wollen wir uns das Törtchen teilen?).

telefon.etymology: Coined by Philipp Reis in 1861 (Telephon) and reinforced in the 1870s by Alexander Graham Bell's English telephone, a neo-classical compound of Ancient Greek tēle- (τῆλε 'far off, distant') and phōnḗ (φωνή 'voice, sound').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Telefon
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Telefon

telefonnummer.etymology: Compound of das Telefon ('telephone', from Greek tēle 'far' + phōnē 'voice') and die Nummer ('number', from Italian numero / Latin numerus). Feminine die Nummer determines the gender.

sources.title: DWDS: Telefonnummer
Wiktionary: Telefonnummer (German)

tempo.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century (initially in fencing, riding, and music, later generalized to 'speed, pace') from Italian tempo ('time, musical beat, pace'), from Latin tempus ('time, season, right moment').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Tempo
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Tempo

teppich.etymology: From Middle High German teppich, tepich and Old High German teppīh, tepid ('woven hanging, tapestry, rug, carpet'), borrowed from Late/Medieval Latin tapētium (Classical Latin tapēte), from Ancient Greek tápēs ('carpet, rug').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Teppich
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Teppich

test.etymology: Borrowed from English test (ultimately from Latin testum, 'earthenware assaying cupel').

history.meaning: earthenware pot -> alchemist's cupel for assaying gold
assaying vessel -> trial of quality, examination
borrowed from English in the 19th/20th c. for a trial or exam

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Test
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Test

test.notes: Both plurals exist in standard German, with die Tests far more common today than older die Teste.

testen.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge record testen (20th c.) as borrowed from English to test, itself from Old French test / Latin testum ('earthenware assaying cupel used to test precious metals').

history.meaning: to put to the proof, try out

cognates.meaning: direct source of the German verb

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): testen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): testen

testen.notes: Because the stem ends in -t, German inserts linking -e- to keep endings audible: du testest, er testet, wir testeten, hat getestet.

teuer.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace teuer through OHG tiuri ('precious, valued, costly') and MHG tiure, exact cognate with English dear.

cognates.meaning: beloved; in British English still also 'expensive' ('too dear')!

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): teuer
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): teuer

teuer.notes: Spelling rule when inflected: teuer drops the unstressed -e- before endings — Das ist teuer, but eine teure Lampe, ein teurer Tisch, teurer als gedacht!

theke.etymology: Borrowed via Latin thēca ('case, box, receptacle', also preserved in Apotheke and Bibliothek) from Ancient Greek thḗkē ('chest, case, counter'), developing in West German usage to 'shop or café counter'.

history.meaning: shop, bakery, or pub counter / bar

cognates.meaning: functional counterpart; French taie ('pillowcase') descends from the same Latin thēca!
native Germanic verb cognate with Greek tithénai ('to put/do') behind thḗkē!

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Theke
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Theke

theke.notes: Spot the hidden Greek family: die Theke ('café/bakery counter'), die Apotheke ('pharmacy'), and die Bibliothek ('library') all share Greek thḗkē ('place where things are set out')!

tief.etymology: From Middle High German tief and Old High German tiof ('deep, profound'), from Proto-Germanic *deupaz ('deep', cognate with English 'deep', Gothic diups), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewb- ('deep, hollow').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): tief
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): tief

tinte.etymology: From Middle High German tinte, tincte and Old High German tincta ('writing ink'), borrowed in monastic scriptoria from Medieval Latin tincta (short for aqua tincta 'dyed/colored water', feminine past participle of Latin tingere 'to dye, dip').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Tinte
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Tinte

tisch.etymology: Old High German tisc and Middle High German tisch were borrowed early from Latin discus / Greek dískos ('round platter, quoit'); because medieval tabletops were lifted onto trestles like large platters, the word came to mean 'table'.

sources.title: DWDS: Tisch
Wiktionary: Tisch (German)

tischdecke.etymology: Determinative compound of Tisch ('table', OHG tisc, MHG tisch, an early borrowing from Latin discus 'disk, platter, table') and Decke ('cover, cloth', OHG decchī, MHG decke, from decken 'to cover').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Tischdecke
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Tischdecke

tischler.etymology: From Late Middle High German tischler, tischer ('cabinetmaker, joiner, carpenter'), occupational agent noun formed with -ler/-er from Tisch ('table, fine furniture', MHG tisch, OHG tisc < Latin discus).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Tischler
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Tischler

titel.etymology: Old High German titul, borrowed from Latin titulus ('inscription, heading, title').

cognates.meaning: via Old French title from the same Latin titulus

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Titel
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Titel

titel.notes: Zero plural: der Titel -> die Titel — names the title of a book, song/track on an album, academic degree, or championship.

toast.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge record Toast ('toasted bread') as a 19th/20th-century borrowing from English toast, which goes back via Old French toster to Latin torrēre / tostum ('to parch, scorch').

history.meaning: toasted bread (or square sandwich loaf); celebratory drink toast

cognates.meaning: browned bread; tribute with raised glass
native Germanic cousins from the same PIE root *ters- ('dry') as Latin torrēre!

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Toast
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Toast

toast.notes: Cultural note: in a German bakery where dense sourdough Brot rules, soft square sliced white bread is specifically called Toastbrot (or ein Toast)!

tod.etymology: From Middle High German and Old High German tōd, tōt ('death'), from Proto-Germanic *dauþuz ('dying, death', cognate with English 'death', Gothic dauþus), a verbal abstract in *-þuz to the root of tot ('dead').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Tod
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Tod

tomatensuppe.etymology: Culinary compound of Tomate ('tomato', plural/combining form Tomaten-, borrowed via Spanish tomate from Nahuatl tomatl) and Suppe ('soup', MHG suppe).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Tomatensuppe
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Tomatensuppe

ton.etymology: In the sense 'musical sound, tone, pitch, accent': from Middle High German tōn, dōn ('melody, tune, sound'), borrowed from Latin tonus ('tension of a string, pitch, tone'), from Ancient Greek tónos ('stretching, cord, pitch', from teínō 'to stretch'). (Homonymous Ton 'clay' continues MHG tāhe, OHG dāha).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Ton
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Ton

tonart.etymology: 18th-century musicological compound of Ton ('tone, pitch') + Art ('kind, mode').

history.meaning: stretching of a string, musical pitch
18th-c. musical term for major/minor key or tonality

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Tonart
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Tonart

tonart.notes: Avoid the literal trap: a piano 'key' you press is die Taste, a door 'key' is der Schlüssel, and a musical 'key' (like D major) is die Tonart!

tonleiter.etymology: 18th-century musical loan translation of Italian scala (musicale) / Latin scāla ('ladder, musical scale'), combining Ton ('musical tone, note', MHG tōn) and Leiter ('ladder', OHG hleitara, MHG leiter).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Tonleiter
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Tonleiter

topf.etymology: Middle High German topf ('deep vessel, pot'), originally a Central and Low German word that spread across standard German.

history.meaning: deep hollow vessel, cooking pot (related to tief 'deep')
cooking pot, saucepan, flowerpot (spread via Luther)

cognates.meaning: related to the Germanic *deup- / *dupp- 'hollow/deep' root behind Topf

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Topf
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Topf

topf.notes: Plural with umlaut: der Topf -> die Töpfe; gives German cuisine's classic comfort dish der Eintopf ('one-pot stew') and proverb Jeder Topf findet seinen Deckel ('Every pot finds its lid').

tor.etymology: In the neuter sense 'gate, large doorway, sports goal': from Middle High German and Old High German tor ('gate, portal'), from Proto-Germanic *durą ('gate, doorway', neuter beside feminine *durz > Tür 'door'), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwer- ('door, courtyard gate').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Tor
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Tor

torklingel.etymology: Compound of Tor ('gate', OHG and MHG tor) and Klingel ('small bell, doorbell', Late MHG klingel, instrument noun from klingeln / klingen 'to ring, tinkle').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Torklingel
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Torklingel

tragen.etymology: From Middle High German tragen and Old High German tragan ('to carry, bear, wear, endure'), from Proto-Germanic *draganą ('to draw, drag, carry', cognate with English 'draw' and 'drag').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): tragen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): tragen

traumcafé.etymology: Compound of Traum ('dream, ideal', OHG and MHG troum, used as an appreciative prefixoid 'dream-, ideal') and Café ('coffeehouse', 18th-c. borrowing from French café).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Traumcafé
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Traumcafé

traurig.etymology: From Middle High German trūrec, trūric and Old High German trūrag ('sad, mournful, downcast'), derived with suffix -ig/-ag from the verb trūren (> trauern 'to mourn, cast down one's eyes', cognate with Old English drēorig 'dreary, sad').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): traurig
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): traurig

treffen.etymology: Nominalized infinitive of the strong verb treffen ('to hit a mark, meet, encounter'), from Middle High German treffen and Old High German treffan ('to hit, strike, touch, concern'), from West Germanic *drepaną ('to strike, hit').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Treffen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Treffen

treppe.etymology: Entered High German from Middle Low German and East Central German treppe ('step, staircase', beside MHG trappe 'step, footprint, stair'), derived from the Germanic root *trap- ('to tread, stamp', cf. trampeln, English 'trap').

history.stage: Middle Low German / Middle High German

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Treppe
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Treppe

treppenabsatz.etymology: Architectural compound of Treppe ('staircase', MHG/MLG treppe, with linking -n-) and Absatz ('landing, ledge, break', from absetzen 'to set down, interrupt', MHG abesetzen), denoting a stair landing.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Treppenabsatz
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Treppenabsatz

tresen.etymology: Entered standard German from Low German Tresen ('shop or bar counter'), from Middle Low German trese, tresor ('treasury, strongbox, merchant's money chest and counter'), borrowed via Old French tresor from Latin thēsaurus (< Greek thēsaurós 'treasure, storehouse').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Tresen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Tresen

trinken.etymology: From Middle High German trinken and Old High German trinkan ('to drink'), from Proto-Germanic *drinkaną ('to drink', cognate with English 'drink', Gothic drigkan).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): trinken
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): trinken

trocken.etymology: From Middle High German trocken, trucken and Old High German trockan, truckan ('dry'), from West Germanic *drukna- / *druknu- ('dry', related by ablaut to Old English drȳge > English 'dry').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): trocken
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): trocken

trocknen.etymology: Old High German trukkanēn, Middle High German truckenen ('to become or make dry'), derived from trocken ('dry').

history.meaning: dry -> to become or make dry

cognates.meaning: related via West Germanic *drūg- ('dry', alongside English dry)

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): trocknen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): trocknen

trocknen.notes: Watch the auxiliar switch in the perfect tense: intransitive 'drying out on its own' takes sein (Die Farbe ist schnell getrocknet), while transitive 'drying something' takes haben (Ich habe die Gläser getrocknet)!

tropfen.etymology: From Middle High German tropfe (reshaped to -en from oblique case endings) and Old High German tropfo ('drop of liquid'), from Proto-Germanic *drupōn- (cognate with English 'drop'), zero-grade noun to the strong verb triefen ('to drip', OHG triofan).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Tropfen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Tropfen

trotzdem.etymology: 19th-century univerbation of the prepositional phrase trotz dem ('in spite of that, nevertheless'), combining the preposition trotz (grammaticalized from the noun Trotz 'defiance', MHG trutz, trotz) and the dative demonstrative pronoun dem.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): trotzdem
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): trotzdem

truhe.etymology: Continues Old High German truha and Middle High German truhe ('heavy lidded wooden chest, coffer, trunk'), from Proto-Germanic *þruhō ('hollowed tree trunk, trough, chest'), cognate with Old English þrūh.

history.meaning: hollowed-out log, wooden chest or coffer

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Truhe
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Truhe

truhe.notes: Originally carved from a single tree trunk — today die Truhe names both an antique hinged wooden chest and a modern top-opening chest freezer (Tiefkühltruhe)!

träumen.etymology: From Middle High German tröumen and Old High German troumen ('to dream'), denominative verb from Traum ('dream', OHG and MHG troum, from Proto-Germanic *draumaz, cognate with English 'dream').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): träumen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): träumen

tschüss.etymology: Entered standard colloquial German via Low German adjüs / atschüs, adapted from Romance farewells (French adieu / Spanish adiós, from Latin ad Deum 'to God').

sources.title: DWDS: tschüss
Wiktionary: tschüss (German)

tuch.etymology: From Middle High German tuoch and Old High German tuoh ('woven cloth, fabric, kerchief'), from West Germanic *dōka- ('cloth', cognate with Old Frisian dōk, Dutch doek).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Tuch
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Tuch

tun.etymology: From Middle High German tuon and Old High German tuon ('to do, make, act, put'), from Proto-Germanic *dōną (cognate with English 'do'), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- ('to put, place, do', cf. Greek títhēmi, Latin facere).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): tun
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): tun

täglich.etymology: From Middle High German tegelīch, tägelīch and Old High German tagalīh ('occurring every day, daily'), derived from Tag ('day', OHG tag) with the adjectival suffix -lich.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): täglich
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): täglich

törtchen.etymology: Diminutive formed with suffix -chen (and umlaut) from Torte ('layered cake, tart', borrowed in the 16th c. via Italian torta from Late Latin tōrta 'round loaf, twisted pastry'), denoting a tartlet or small pastry.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Törtchen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Törtchen

tür.etymology: Continues Old High German turi and Middle High German tür (originally dual/plural forms for double-leaf doors), cognate with English 'door' and related to neuter das Tor ('gate').

sources.title: DWDS: Tür
Wiktionary: Tür (German)

türschlüssel.etymology: Determinative compound of Tür ('door', OHG turi) and Schlüssel ('key', OHG sluzzil, from schließen 'to lock'), recorded in DWDS/Pfeifer under Türschlüssel.

morphemes.meaning: key ('locker', instrument noun in -el of schließen)

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Türschlüssel
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Türschlüssel

türschlüssel.notes: Zero plural: der Türschlüssel -> die Türschlüssel; notice how der Schlüssel ('key') and das Schloss ('lock') both come from schließen ('to close/lock').

tüte.etymology: Borrowed into standard German from Middle Low German tūte ('horn, cone-shaped cornet of rolled paper'), originally denoting a conical paper packet used by grocers.

history.meaning: animal horn, blowing horn -> rolled paper cone used by grocers
conical candy bag -> any paper or plastic shopping bag

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Low German/Dutch tuten ('to blow a horn'), same root!

rootFamily.gloss: giant cone of treats given on a child's first day of school!

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Tüte
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Tüte

tüte.notes: Its original 'cone' shape still shines through in die Schultüte (first-graders' giant cardboard cone) and die Eistüte ('ice-cream cone') — Note: Austrians say das Sackerl instead of die Tüte!

uff.etymology: Expressive, onomatopoeic interjection imitating an audible exhalation or sigh of relief, exhaustion, or effort (attested since Early New High German, with parallels across European languages such as French ouf).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): uff
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): uff

uhr.etymology: Entered High German in the 14th/15th century from Middle Low German ūre ('hour; timepiece, clock'), borrowed via Old French ore, ure from Latin hōra ('hour, time of day'), from Ancient Greek hṓra ('season, time, hour').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Uhr
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Uhr

uhrmacher.etymology: Early New High German compound of Uhr ('clock, watch', via Middle Low German ūre from Latin hōra) and Macher ('maker', from machen).

history.meaning: craftsman who builds and repairs clocks and watches

cognates.meaning: from the same Latin/Greek hōra that gave German Uhr ('clock')!

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Uhrmacher
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Uhrmacher

uhrmacher.notes: Remember German's time split: eine Stunde is a 60-minute duration ('an hour'), while die Uhr is the timepiece ('clock/watch') or clock-time (drei Uhr = 'three o'clock').

um.etymology: From Old High German umbi and Middle High German umbe ('around, on both sides'). In modern German it marks spatial encirclement, exact clock hours (um zwölf Uhr), and purpose clauses with zu.

sources.title: DWDS: um
Wiktionary: um (German)

umbau.etymology: Deverbal compound noun from umbauen ('to rebuild, remodel, alter a structure'), combining um- ('around, anew', OHG umbi) and Bau ('building, construction', OHG and MHG bū).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Umbau
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Umbau

umbuchen.etymology: Separable prefix verb from um- ('over, to another entry/reservation') and buchen ('to enter into an account book, book, reserve', derived from Buch 'book, ledger', OHG buoh).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): umbuchen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): umbuchen

umdrehen.etymology: Separable prefix verb from Middle High German umbedræjen ('to turn around, rotate, invert'), combining um- ('around', OHG umbi) and drehen ('to turn, twist', OHG drāen, MHG dræjen).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): umdrehen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): umdrehen

umknicken.etymology: Separable prefix verb from um- ('over, down') and knicken ('to bend sharply with a crack, snap, buckle', entered High German in the 16th/17th c. from Low German knicken, an expressive/onomatopoeic verb). Commonly used of twisting an ankle or folding over.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): umknicken
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): umknicken

umrühren.etymology: Separable prefix verb from Middle High German umberüeren ('to stir around, mix'), combining um- ('around', OHG umbi) and rühren ('to stir, move, touch', OHG ruoren, MHG rüeren).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): umrühren
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): umrühren

umschauen.etymology: Separable prefix verb from Middle High German umbeschouwen ('to look around, survey'), combining um- ('around', OHG umbi) and schauen ('to look, gaze', OHG scouwōn, MHG schouwen).

weiß.etymology: From Middle High German wīz and Old High German hwīz, wīz ('shining, bright, white'), from Proto-Germanic *hwītaz ('white', cognate with English 'white', Gothic hveits), from Proto-Indo-European *kweyd- ('to shine, bright, white', cf. Sanskrit śvetá-).

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): weiß

welcher.etymology: From Middle High German welch, welich and Old High German hwelīh, welīh ('of what sort, which'), from Proto-Germanic *hwalīkaz ('having what form, which', cognate with English 'which', Gothic hveleiks), a compound of the interrogative stem *hwa- ('what, who') and *līką ('body, form').

welt.etymology: From Middle High German welt, werlt and Old High German weralt ('age of man, lifetime, humanity, the inhabited earth, world'), from West Germanic *wira-aldiz (cognate with Old English weorold > English 'world'), a compound of *wiraz ('man', cf. Latin vir, Werwolf) and *aldiz ('age, generation', related to alt 'old').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Welt
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Welt

wenig.etymology: From Middle High German wēnec, wēnic ('lamentable, weak, small, little, few') and Old High German wēnag ('wretched, miserable, lamentable, small'), derived with suffix -ag/-ig from the interjection wē ('woe!') or weinōn ('to weep'); the sense shifted from 'pitiful, small' to 'little, few'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): wenig
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): wenig

wenn.etymology: From Middle High German wenne, wanne and Old High German hwanne, wenne ('when, whenever, if'), an umlauted/front-vowel variant of wann (< Proto-Germanic *hwannē); in New High German, wenn specialized to conditional and iterative temporal clauses ('if, whenever'), while wann remained interrogative.

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): wenn

wer.etymology: From Middle High German wer and Old High German hwer, wer ('who'), from Proto-Germanic *hwaz (cognate with English 'who', Gothic hvas), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷós ('who', cf. Latin quis, Sanskrit káḥ).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): wer
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): wer

werden.etymology: From Middle High German werden and Old High German werdan ('to turn into, come to be, become, happen'), from Proto-Germanic *werþaną ('to turn, become', cognate with Old English weorþan), from Proto-Indo-European *wert- ('to turn, rotate', cf. Latin vertere).

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): werden

werfen.etymology: From Middle High German werfen and Old High German werfan ('to throw, cast, hurl'), from Proto-Germanic *werpaną ('to throw, twist', cognate with English 'warp'), from Proto-Indo-European *werb- ('to turn, bend, fling').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Werkzeugkasten

werner.etymology: From the Old High German dithematic masculine given name Warinhari, Werinheri (Middle High German Wernher), composed of the Germanic ethnonymic/stem element *Warin- (the Warnen, a Germanic tribe, or *warō 'protection, guard') and *harjaz (OHG heri 'army, warrior', > Heer).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): wertvoll

wetter.etymology: From Middle High German weter and Old High German wetar ('weather, open air, wind, storm'), from Proto-Germanic *wedrą ('wind, weather', cognate with English 'weather'), built with instrument/medio-passive suffix *-þrą on the PIE root *h₂weh₁- ('to blow', cf. wehen, Wind).

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Wetter

wetterbericht.etymology: 19th-century compound of Wetter ('weather', OHG wetar, MHG weter) and Bericht ('report, account', Late MHG beriht 'settlement, instruction, report', from berichten 'to set right, inform'), denoting a weather report or forecast.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Wetterbericht
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Wetterbericht

wichtig.etymology: From Late Middle High German wihtec and Middle Low German wichtich ('having heavy weight, weighty; figuratively significant, important'), derived with suffix -ig from Gewicht / Wicht ('weight', MHG gewihte, wiht, from wiegen 'to weigh').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): wichtig

zahlend.etymology: Present participle of zahlen ('to pay', MHG zaln, OHG zalōn), meaning 'paying' (as in zahlender Gast 'paying guest').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zahlend
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zahlend

zedernkiste.etymology: Compound of Zeder ('cedar', OHG zēdarboum from Latin cedrus / Greek kédros) + Kiste ('box, chest', OHG kista from Latin cista); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Zeder and Kiste.

zehe.etymology: From Middle High German zēhe, Old High German zēha ('toe'), from Proto-Germanic *taihwōn- (cognate with English toe).

rootFamily.gloss: to point, show (from the same PIE root!)

zehn.etymology: From Middle High German zehen, zēn and Old High German zehan ('ten'), from Proto-Germanic *tehun (cognate with English 'ten', Gothic taihun), from Proto-Indo-European *dékm̥ ('ten', cf. Latin decem, Greek déka).

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zehnmal

cognates.meaning: ordinal of ten (and archaic tithe < Old English tēogoþa)

history.meaning: to mark with a sign, indicate (from *taikną 'sign')

cognates.meaning: exact cognate of base noun Zeichen (< *taikną)!

Latin dīcere, Greek deíknȳmi).
